abstract: Genomic imprinting results in parent-of-origin-dependent gene expression and plays an important role in endosperm development. The type I MADS-box transcription factor PHERES1 (PHE1) has been implicated in the regulation of imprinted genes, particularly paternally expressed genes (PEGs). Silencing of the maternal alleles of PEGs is mediated by repressive histone modifications, including H3K27me3 established by the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2). Here, we established an adapted low-input CUT&Tag protocol to profile the allele-specific genome-wide binding of PHE1 in the endosperm and compared the resulting binding profiles with previously published ChIP-seq data. Our CUT&Tag analysis substantially recapitulated the previously identified PHE1-binding landscape while requiring considerably less input material. Consistent with earlier findings, PHE1 binding was enriched at RC/Helitron transposable elements and imprinted genes, specifically PEGs. Interestingly, most PHE1-bound PEGs exhibited binding on both maternal and paternal alleles despite H3K27me3 enrichment on their maternal alleles. Perturbation of H3K27me3 deposition did not alter the predominantly biallelic PHE1 occupancy observed at these loci, supporting that PHE1 binding can persist in an H3K27me3-associated chromatin environment. In contrast, analysis of gene expression in fertilization independent seed (fis) prc2 mutants impaired in H3K27me3 establishment caused increased expression of PHE1 targets and altered their parent-of-origin-specific expression patterns. Our findings reveal that biallelic transcription factor occupancy can coexist with parent-of-origin-specific transcriptional regulation, highlighting the importance of chromatin context in determining the transcriptional output of PHE1-bound genes.
